1:
Whether the informers acted for themselves or on a hint from the court is the first thing the commentators try to settle. Gill thinks it cannot be made certain, but leans to their own initiative, since men who had once tried to betray David had reason to fear what he would remember when he came to the throne, and so wanted him cut off by another hand. Henry inclines the other way, that Saul may well have let them know under-hand that the design continued; and if he did not, they were officious men who knew what would please him and had despaired of reconciliation with David. His further thought is that Saul, left alone, might have stayed in the better mind he showed at the cave, which turns the incident into an argument for praying that the sparks of temptation be kept from the tinder we already carry. Keil and Delitzsch date the second betrayal after the marriage with Abigail and the return to the desert of Judah, and add that before Jeshimon was given more exactly in the earlier chapter as south of the wilderness.

On the march itself the question is why so large a force. Clarke makes it a calculation: the king knew David had six hundred men, judged it unsafe to pursue so able a general with fewer, and took men picked from the whole army so that he could depend on them. Ellicott needs no calculation, since the three thousand look like the standing force kept about the king in the Gibeah garrison, and he supposes the advice to take the field came from Abner. Gill has the king rise at once, glad of the opportunity and perhaps regretting that he had not seized David at the cave; Henry puts the same promptness more sharply, as unsanctified hearts losing the good impressions their convictions had made and returning to what they had just renounced.

David's conduct is read as deliberate restraint. Henry observes that he did not march out to meet the army but sought his own safety and not the king's ruin, and that curbing the bravery of his own spirit by a silent retirement showed more true valour than any irregular resistance; David would not believe the king could deal so basely until he had the strongest evidence, which is why the spies were sent. Gill makes the same point doctrinally, that a man who knew the Lord would protect him still thought it proper to be on his guard and to use the means. Ellicott supplies the misjudgement underneath it, that after the protestations at En-gedi David probably expected to be left in peace, forgetting the man he dealt with and how likely the old mania was to return. Keil and Delitzsch fill in the reconnaissance, the king lying by the waggon rampart with the fighting men encamped round him, and identify the two attendants: Ahimelech the Hittite is never heard of again, while Abishai, son of David's sister and brother to Joab, became one of the celebrated generals of the reign.

Ellicott alone asks what the chapter is doing in the book at all. He sets out the resemblances to the earlier sparing of the king, the same informers, the same three thousand from Gibeah, the same urging, the same refusal, the same token taken from the sleeping king and the same short-lived repentance, and then the difference he judges decisive, a night raid on a camp against a midday rest in a cave; Ewald and De Wette he reports on the other side. His graver question he cannot answer, why a compiler who studies conciseness everywhere else should give two long accounts of the same kind of act, and the most he will suggest is that whatever told for the glory of Israel's hero was of the deepest interest to the people.
5:
Where the king was lying is a question about one Hebrew word. Clarke gives the whole range: a ring of carriages, the circle formed by the troops, or, with Luther, a fortress made of wagons, and since the root means anything round it might even be a round pavilion; the Arabs, he notes, still pitch in a circle, their principal officers in the centre. Ellicott settles for the barricade of baggage wagons, recording that the Greek made it covered chariots and that Keil read a wagon rampart, and Henry has the king in his chariot among the carriages, his spear stuck in the ground beside him, ready if the camp should be beaten up in the night. Gill and Clarke both explain how the camp could be studied at all: David came near enough to take in the arrangement with his naked eye, and men who knew the country could watch the army often without being discovered. Wesley repeats the judgement that the king would probably have pursued no further if the informers had not set him on.

Who went down, and why only two, is answered three ways. Gill holds that Josephus is wrong to send both attendants, since David chose one for secrecy, and calls it a bold enterprise for two men to enter a camp of three thousand when the sentinels at least could not be presumed asleep. Henry supposes the other man either declined the adventure as too dangerous or was content that the readier kinsman should run the risk; Ellicott says plainly that he backed out, while Abishai volunteered at once with the reckless gallantry that marked those kinsmen all their lives. On the motive behind the raid the three divide. Henry will not choose between natural courage, an extraordinary impression on the spirit, and the oracle, but says that David went through the guards as Gideon did, on a special assurance of protection. Gill is certain it was not courage but the Spirit of God, given for a second occasion of convincing the king of his innocence, and Wesley makes it a special instinct, with the possibility that David was told beforehand of the sleep that had fallen on the camp.

The sleeping camp is where Henry's comment gathers. He observes that the men set to keep watch were as fast asleep as the rest, that nothing but a deep sleep from the Lord accounts for two men walking and talking among three thousand without one stirring, and that sleep which is rest and refreshment to God's beloved can be made a prison to his enemies. His conclusion is that the strongest are easily weakened, the wisest befooled and the most watchful baffled, so that an army lies there in effect disarmed and chained while nothing at all is done to it.

The offer to kill the king is given its exact force by those who weigh the words. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both read the second clause as meaning that one stroke would be thorough enough to need no second, Ellicott borrowing Lange's rendering of pinning the man to the ground and both citing the Latin to the same effect. Clarke notices that the words are those David's men had used in the cave at En-gedi, and that the answer given is the same answer as before. Ellicott takes the occasion of the names to trace the Hittites from Abraham's dealings near Hebron through a conquest that subdued without exterminating them, which is how a Hittite comes to be among David's trusted men and how Uriah later held a post in the army; of this one nothing more is heard. His other excursus is the blood feud: Abner, who dreaded in David's accession the ruin of Saul's house and his own captaincy, afterwards killed the youngest of these brothers and was himself murdered by the other two.
9:
The refusal rests on the anointing, and two voices set out what that meant. Ellicott holds that David, taught no doubt by Samuel, regarded the king's person as made sacred and inviolable by the oil, so that the man had become Jehovah's property and only Jehovah could lawfully take the life; he adds the possibility that these sentiments about the rights of kings were not spoken in the dark among sleeping soldiers but afterwards, when the two were going over the night's work together. Wesley puts the same thing as a subject's reasoning, that a tyrant is still lord and king, and that a man already designated to the throne is for the present a subject who may neither kill him nor consent to another doing it. Gill notes only that the order was laid on Abishai with the utmost abhorrence of the thing forbidden.

The three alternatives David offers instead are counted the same way by both who take them up. Clarke calls them the three ordinary ways in which a man finishes his day as a hireling, a stroke of divine judgment, a natural death that must in the course of things come before his own, or a fall by his country's enemies, and concludes that murder could not be lawful, since it would take the matter out of God's hand. Ellicott makes the first of them a sudden death by disease, with the recent end of Nabal no doubt in the speaker's mind, and thinks an arrow sent by an unseen hand was what he had in view for the third.

The two things carried off are read as regalia or as camp furniture. Ellicott treats the spear as the king's especial sign of royalty and cites the judgement that taking it from his head was an omen of the kingdom passing to David; on the cruse he quotes Ewald for an ancient usage by which a high officer kept a costly ewer for the king's washing and carried it on campaign, so that its loss would disgrace him almost as much as losing his sceptre. Ewald's wider point he reports too, that the founder of a new dynasty is often shown receiving some symbol of royalty from his predecessor by accident or in sport, as Alexander takes the royal divining cup, and that the belief in omens was nowhere stronger than in high affairs of state. Clarke answers all of this with the plain practice of a camp, that every Arab has his lance stuck in the ground beside him so as to be ready in a moment, and that the cruse is no more than the canteen a man must carry where water is scarce. Gill is interested in neither question but in who did the carrying, and thinks David took the things himself, either because Abishai declined to touch what he might not kill, or because David thought better of leaving a spear in that man's hand so near the sleeping king.

Whether the sleep was a miracle is the chapter's open question. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase to mean a deep sleep sent from the Lord and let it stand at that, and Clarke sharpens it by noting that the word is the one used of the sleep God caused to fall on Adam. Ellicott grants that the first impression is of a supernatural drowsiness and then argues that no special miracle need be supposed: the army lay in a friendly district and never dreamed of a surprise, the men on duty may well have been drinking, and the two intruders were practised scouts after years of flight. His evidence is the sarcasm with which David afterwards rebukes the general, which shows that what stayed in his memory was carelessness. Ellicott also prefers the blunter Hebrew of the record, that none saw, and none knew, and none awaked.
13:
The distance David put between himself and the camp is read for its meaning as well as its geography. Gill has him cross the valley between the two hills, perhaps a brook in it, and cites Josephus for the brook and the mountain top. Keil and Delitzsch make the notice that the hill was far off a mark of accurate tradition, and draw an inference from it: at the cave David had followed the king out and called after him at close range, whereas now he reckoned much less on any change of mind and rather feared being seized as soon as the king woke. Ellicott takes the same point from Keil, adding that far off means across a steep ravine rather than in a straight line, and has the shrill cry wake a sentinel who roused the general. Wesley keeps to the practical explanation, that the voice would carry a great distance in clear air and the silence of the night while the speaker stayed out of reach, and Henry says the position was chosen so that they might hear him and not reach him.

Henry's note at this point runs on through the whole exchange, and his treatment of the general is the sharpest in the chapter. He takes the opening question to mean a man in office, bound by the duty of his place to inspect the soldiery, and turns it into the taunt that a general should not be a sluggard. He thinks the guards woke easily enough once David was out of danger, a voice at a great distance rousing men whom nothing in the camp had disturbed, which he reads as proof that the hand of God had locked them in sleep. His two charges are that the general had lost his honour and deserved to lose his head, since whoever could carry off the spear could as easily have carried off the life, so that the question of who were the king's best friends answers itself. His moral is that those who unjustly condemn others are sometimes justly left to fall into condemnation themselves.

How far the guards were really culpable is disputed. Gill calls it a great fault if no watch had been set, the business of a general, and notes that the rebuke is phrased as less than it means. Keil and Delitzsch have the taunt charge Abner with making himself answerable for his master's death, and hold that the reproaches were aimed past him at the king, who might hear and did hear, to show that his most faithful defender was the man he was hunting. Clarke takes the opposite view of the men's guilt: the address is a strong irony and calls them sons of death, but they were not to blame, their neglect being the effect of a supernatural sleep, and he thinks Saul would have put the general and his chief officers to death had he not been so deeply affected by David's generosity.

The wording of the challenge draws two further notes. Ellicott defends the translators for rendering the Hebrew word as valiant, since it is used elsewhere in the nobler sense that sets great men against mean ones, and he finds in the bitterness of the whole address the sign of a deadly feud, which makes David's later friendship with this man and his grief at his death the more generous. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the general's retort as a complaint about the shouting itself, that the noise offends the king and breaks his rest, and Ellicott cites the Latin to the same effect. Gill's only addition is that the man hailed had the next post in the army and had not behaved worthily of it.
17:
The recognition is a matter of voice and not of sight. Gill observes that the general had not known who was calling, as his own question shows, while the king knew at once, being by then awake from the exchange he had been hearing. Ellicott calls the account natural on this very point: the raid was made at night, the return at the dawn of early morning, and a man could hear a voice he had once dearly loved without making out the figure on the far ridge. He adds what the morning light would have shown, the royal spear glittering in the speaker's hand, proof enough that the son of Jesse was not seeking the king's life. Gill reads the opening complaint as an argument from interest as well as duty: pursuing a servant who would gladly have gone on serving was beneath the king and against his own advantage, and the man was hunted as a traitor without known offence.

The offering David proposes is the hardest clause in the chapter, and four readings of it are offered. Clarke offers two: either that God should take his life at the king's hand and accept it as a sacrifice, or, since the word is the gratitude-offering, that God should accept the king's thanks for purging the land of an evildoer, which would hold only if David were one. Ellicott reports Wordsworth's smoother version, drawn through the Arabic of the Targum, in which David asks to be told his offence and offers to bring a sacrifice for it. The sense Ellicott thinks most scholars take is blunter, that if God really is behind this, let him smell an offering, which is to say, let the king pray that the temptation be taken from him. Wesley makes the sacrifice a joint one, offered by both men to turn away a wrath that lies on both.

Behind the clause lies the question whether God sets a man on to do evil, and Ellicott faces it directly. He traces the conception through the hardening of Pharaoh's heart and the evil spirit sent on this very king, and cites Payne Smith: Israel held God to be the one power by which all things are done, without its following that whatever providence seems to lead to is right for a man, since every such leading must be judged by God's unchanging law. His own account is that the Spirit pleaded long and in vain until it was quenched and took its flight, after which the deserted heart hardens and the swept and garnished shrine stands empty for another tenant.

The complaint about exile and the two images at the end are handled in very different styles. Clarke and Wesley both read the driving out as a sentence to idolatry, the one because leaving the tabernacle for a refuge among idolaters says in effect go and serve other gods, the other because a man so placed may be ensnared by their counsels or forced by their power. Ellicott makes the fear of dying far from the land the Lord loves the thought that governed David's later life, and the reason the bringing up of the Ark became his dream. On the last plea the readings divide: Gill and Wesley take it as a warning that God sees spilt blood and will avenge it, Gill noting that it can also be rendered as a confidence that his blood shall not fall at all, while Ellicott prefers far from the presence of the Lord and makes it a plea against an exile's death. Clarke ends with the observation he owes to Harmer, that Arabs hunt partridges by putting them up again and again until the birds are too weary to fly and can be clubbed, which is how the king had hunted David; Ellicott adds from Conder that partridges still tenant those cliffs.
21:
The confession is weighed word by word. Gill notes that it goes further than anything the king had admitted before, and still doubts it, since a guilty conscience may force such words from a man as it did from Pharaoh without any real sense of sin. Clarke suggests the verb might be rendered I have erred, or I have been mistaken, which would mean only that the king had taken David for a very different man. Ellicott hears something besides sorrow in it, and follows the Dean of Canterbury in taking the self-reproach to be for having put himself in David's power a second time through overweening confidence, with the unguarded camp before his eyes. Henry reads a double fault, against God's law in the sinning and against the king's own interest in the folly, since the man he hunted would have been among his best friends.

Whether any of it was sincere divides the voices, and only one takes the favourable side. Henry grants that the king meant what he said in the mood he was then in, and still holds that neither the confession nor the promise came from a principle of true repentance. Keil and Delitzsch call it a good intention never carried out, and quote a devotional comment to the effect that a man who keeps promising not to do again what he does again should rather take refuge with God for grace, and might have asked David himself to pray for him. Ellicott finds a ring of falseness in both the apology and the blessing, and thinks that was the impression made on David, who declined the invitation without a word and soon left the kingdom. Wesley stands alone in taking the repentance at face value, that God touched the king's heart and that he never attempted the pursuit again.

The returning of the spear and the appeal that follows are read as one act of self-restraint. Gill thinks the spear may have served as a sceptre, which is why David would not keep it, lest anyone say he had taken an ensign of royalty and meant to seize the throne. Keil and Delitzsch have him send a servant for it and turn the matter over to the recompense of God, and they defend the closing words against Thenius, who heard in them the sounding of David's own praises: they are rather the testimony of a good conscience before an enemy who admits his wrong without feeling any need of forgiveness. Clarke finds a vast dignity in the speech, since David neither begs his life nor argues at all, but leaves the case to God as the vindicator of oppressed innocence.

The parting is given its weight by all of them. Clarke prefers the Chaldee version of the doubled Hebrew idiom, that in reigning David should reign and in prospering prosper, and notices that the king is left with nothing to say beyond his admission while not one officer speaks for his master, since they could see which man was under God's keeping. Ellicott passes on Wordsworth's comparison, that the king is here among the prophets again in spite of himself, foretelling the exaltation he dreaded, with the exclamation of Julian set beside it. Gill and Wesley both take the blessing as real so far as it went, Gill that the king believed David would prosper, Wesley that the conviction was strong enough to make him applaud David and condemn himself in his own soldiers' hearing. Ellicott closes where the history closes, with the two men one prophet had anointed parting for the last time, never to see each other again, not even when the men of Jabesh Gilead had risked their lives for the body and could do nothing for it but burn it.
